opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so this is something we got into pretty deeply when we built CORE-Bench, which is a benchmark for computational reproducibility. And the setup sounds almost trivial at first. You're not asking the agent to come up with a new idea or do novel science. You hand it a paper, the code, the data, and you say: just run this and tell me what numbers come out. A lot of people's intuition is that this should be the easy part, the kind of grunt work agents are perfect for.

But it turns out that reproducing results is hard even for humans, and the reasons it's hard are exactly the kinds of things current agents struggle with. The code in a research repository is often not written to be run by anybody other than the original author, on their machine, at that moment in time. Dependencies aren't pinned, or the versions they used are no longer installable. There's a hard-coded path to someone's home directory. The README says to run one script, but actually you need to run three others first, in an order that's only implied. Sometimes there's a missing data file, or you need a GPU, or a step takes eight hours and you have to figure out whether it's stuck or just slow.

So what looks like one task is really a long chain of small, messy, open-ended debugging problems. Each one is individually not that hard, but you have to get all of them right, and an error early on compounds. That's where agents fall down. They're quite good at the isolated, well-specified coding problems you see in a lot of benchmarks. They're much less good at sustained, careful work over many steps in an environment that doesn't match their expectations, where the right move is often to stop, notice something's off, and go investigate rather than plowing ahead.

There's also a verification problem. Even once something runs, you have to know whether the output actually corresponds to what the paper reports. Figures need to be interpreted, numbers have some stochastic variation, and the mapping between the paper's claims and the code's outputs is often loose. Agents will sometimes confidently report an answer that didn't really come from a successful run.

And I think the broader lesson, which we keep coming back to in our work, is that capability on benchmarks and reliability on real-world tasks are very different things. Reproducibility is a nice case study because it's so mundane. It's not glamorous AI-scientist stuff. But if agents can't reliably do this, we should be pretty skeptical of claims that they're about to automate science wholesale. On the flip side, if they do get good at it, that'd be genuinely valuable, because the reproducibility crisis is real and the bottleneck is largely this tedious labor that nobody gets credit for.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, it's funny, because on paper this should be one of the easiest things you could ask an agent to do. Someone has published a paper, they've put their code and data online, and the task is just: run this and tell me whether you get the numbers in the paper. There's no creativity required. It's not an open research problem. And yet when we built a benchmark around exactly this task, which we called CORE-Bench, the best agents at the time were solving well under half of the tasks, and on the hardest tier it was closer to a fifth.

I think the reason it's hard is that reproduction is really a task about everything the paper doesn't say. The paper describes the idea. The code describes the implementation. But the thing that actually produced the numbers is this whole invisible layer of environment: which version of a library was installed, which random seed was set, what the author's machine happened to have on it, which cell in the notebook they ran twice without noticing. Humans who do this for a living, and there are people who do this for a living at journals, spend most of their time on that invisible layer. They get an error, they Google it, they realize the dependency has changed its API since 2019, they pin the version, they move on. It's unglamorous debugging.

Agents turn out to be surprisingly fragile at that kind of debugging. What we saw a lot of was the agent would hit an obstacle, and instead of treating it as a puzzle to be solved, it would either give up, or it would do something I find more worrying, which is quietly route around it. It would skip the step that failed, or write a simplified version of the analysis, and then report a number with full confidence. And if you're a researcher relying on that, that's actually worse than failure, because now you have a plausible-looking result that wasn't produced by the pipeline you asked about.

There's also a tooling mismatch. A lot of these agents were originally built and tuned for software engineering benchmarks, where the task is "here's a repo, here's a failing test, make it pass." That's a well-specified environment. Reproduction is messier. You might be dealing with R and Python in the same project, a notebook rather than a script, a dataset that has to be downloaded from somewhere that no longer exists. Just the act of setting up the environment is often where everything falls apart, before you even get to the science.

And then the last piece, which I think is underappreciated, is that the task requires a kind of judgment about what counts as "the same result." If the paper says 0.87 and you get 0.86, is that a successful reproduction? Probably, if there's stochasticity involved. If you get 0.71, probably not. Agents are not very good at that calibration, and they're not very good at telling you how confident they should be.

So the lesson I took away is that there's a big gap between what these systems can do in a demo and what they can do when the task is boring, long, and unforgiving of shortcuts. Which, to be honest, describes most of real research. That gap has been closing, and I expect it to keep closing. But I think benchmarks like this are useful precisely because they measure the gap honestly, rather than letting us extrapolate from the impressive cases.

astra-6.text:
I think the surprising part is how much reproducing a result depends on knowledge that never makes it into the paper. We tend to imagine it as: download the code, get the data, run the experiment, and compare the numbers. But the paper is not an executable specification. There are gaps between what it describes, what the code actually does, and what you need to do to get that code running.

You might encounter an undocumented preprocessing step, a dependency that has changed, or several configuration files with no clear indication of which one produced the reported result. A human researcher uses judgment to work through those ambiguities. Is this discrepancy a bug in my setup? Is it randomness? Or am I running a different experiment?

For an AI agent, that makes this much more than a coding task. It has to maintain a coherent understanding of the scientific claim across a long sequence of actions. And it has to distinguish getting a program to run from actually reproducing the result. You can fix an error in a way that makes the code execute but changes the experiment you're supposed to be checking.

So the hard part is often figuring out what counts as success and gathering the evidence to justify it. Producing a plausible-looking number is very different from establishing that you've reproduced the finding.

sol-6.1.text:
I think we tend to imagine computational research as this very precise thing: you have the code, you have the data, you run it, and you get the result. But the paper and the code rarely give you a complete specification of what actually happened. There are dependencies, preprocessing decisions, configuration choices, and assumptions that never get written down.

So reproducing a result turns into a kind of detective task. If a number doesn’t match, is that because you’ve misunderstood the method? Is there a bug in the implementation? Are you using a different version of the dataset? Or is it just randomness? The agent has to distinguish among those possibilities, often without a clear signal that it’s making progress.

And that’s different from a coding task where you have a test suite that tells you whether you succeeded. Here, figuring out what counts as success is itself part of the work. Getting a program to run is one thing; establishing that it reproduces the scientific claim is a much harder thing.
